stem: What is a siphon?

options.content: A tube full of liquid that carries liquid from a container up over its edge and down to a lower level
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: A pump that lifts water from a deep borehole
options.rationale: A siphon needs no pump.

options.content: A cylinder that multiplies a force using oil
options.rationale: That is a hydraulic system.

options.content: A valve that lets liquid flow one way only
options.rationale: That is a valve.

explanation: A siphon is a tube, full of liquid, that carries liquid over a barrier to a lower level without a pump.

stem: Which condition is necessary for a siphon to empty a tank of water?

options.content: The outlet end of the tube must be lower than the water surface in the tank.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The tube must be made of metal.
options.rationale: Any airtight tube works.

options.content: The top of the bend must be at least 10 m above the water.
options.rationale: The bend must be less than about 10 m above the water surface.

options.content: The tube must contain some air before it is placed in the tank.
options.rationale: The tube must be completely full of water.

explanation: Water flows only if the outlet is below the surface of the water in the tank, and the tube must start full of water.

stem: A siphon will keep emptying a tank if its outlet end is lifted above the level of the water in the tank.
explanation: False. The outlet must be below the water surface in the tank. If it is raised above that level, the pressure is greater on the outlet side and the water flows back into the tank.

stem: What pushes the water up the short arm of a siphon, from the tank to the top of the bend?

options.content: Atmospheric pressure acting on the water surface in the tank
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Suction created by the water falling down the long arm
options.rationale: Suction is not a force; the push comes from atmospheric pressure.

options.content: The weight of the water in the short arm
options.rationale: Weight acts downwards and opposes the rise.

options.content: Capillary action in the tube
options.rationale: Capillary rise is tiny in a wide tube.

explanation: The pressure at the top of the tube is lower than atmospheric pressure, so the atmosphere pressing on the water surface in the tank pushes water up the short arm.
hints: What presses down on the open water surface in the tank?

stem: A siphon carries water out of a tank and pours it onto the ground well below the tank. The inlet end of the tube is held near the bottom of the tank. When will the flow stop?

options.content: When the water level in the tank falls to the inlet, so that air enters the tube
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: When the tank is half empty, because the pressure has halved
options.rationale: The flow continues as long as the tube stays full and the outlet is below the water surface.

options.content: After a fixed time of about one minute
options.rationale: There is no fixed time.

options.content: Never: it will also empty the water below the inlet
options.rationale: Once air enters the tube, the siphon stops.

explanation: The siphon keeps flowing while the tube is full of water and the outlet is below the water surface. When the water level reaches the inlet, air enters and the column of water breaks.
hints: What happens to the tube when the water surface drops below its open end?

stem: Why must a siphon tube be completely filled with liquid before it is started?

options.content: So that the tube becomes heavy enough to stay in place.
options.rationale: The weight of the tube is not the reason.

options.content: Because a full tube is under higher pressure than the atmosphere.
options.rationale: The pressure at the top of the tube is lower than atmospheric.

options.content: To clean the inside of the tube.
options.rationale: Cleaning is not the reason.

options.content: So that there is an unbroken column of liquid; air in the tube stops the flow.
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: The siphon works only with a continuous column of liquid from the inlet to the outlet. Air in the tube breaks the column and the flow stops.

stem: What happens to the pressure applied to one part of an enclosed liquid?

options.content: It is lost as the liquid is compressed.
options.rationale: Liquids are almost incompressible.

options.content: It acts only in the direction of the applied force.
options.rationale: Pressure in a fluid acts in all directions.

options.content: It is passed on equally to every part of the liquid.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: It doubles at the far end of the pipe.
options.rationale: It is passed on equally, not increased.

explanation: Pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally throughout the liquid. This is the principle of every hydraulic system.

stem: Why do hydraulic systems use a liquid such as oil rather than air?

options.content: Liquids are lighter than air.
options.rationale: Liquids are much denser than air.

options.content: Air cannot exert pressure.
options.rationale: Air does exert pressure, but it is easily compressed.

options.content: Oil makes the pistons rust.
options.rationale: Oil prevents rust, but that is not the main reason.

options.content: Liquids are almost incompressible, so pressure is passed on instead of squashing the fluid.
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: A liquid hardly changes volume when squeezed, so pushing one piston moves the other at once. Air would just be compressed.

stem: A force of $60\ \text{N}$ acts on a small piston of area $0.0015\ \text{m}^2$ in a hydraulic system. What is the pressure in the liquid?

In a hydraulic press an effort of $120\ \text{N}$ acts on a small piston of area $2.5\ \text{cm}^2$. The large piston has an area of $75\ \text{cm}^2$. Calculate the force exerted by the large piston.
explanation: Pressure $= \dfrac{120}{2.5} = 48\ \text{N/cm}^2$. Force on large piston $= 48 \times 75 = 3600\ \text{N}$.
hints: Find the pressure first: p = F ÷ A for the small piston.
Then F = p × A for the large piston.

stem: In a hydraulic system the small piston has an area of $2.0\ \text{cm}^2$ and the large piston an area of $60\ \text{cm}^2$. The small piston is pushed down $12\ \text{cm}$. How far does the large piston rise?
explanation: Volume of liquid moved $= 2.0 \times 12 = 24\ \text{cm}^3$. Rise of large piston $= \dfrac{24}{60} = 0.4\ \text{cm}$.
workedSolution: 1. Volume of liquid moved $= 2.0 \times 12 = 24\ \text{cm}^3$. Rise of large piston $= \dfrac{24}{60} = 0.4\ \text{cm}$.
hints: The volume of liquid pushed out of the small cylinder equals the volume that enters the large one.

stem: A hydraulic jack has a pump piston of area $1.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2$ and a ram (large piston) of area $4.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$. The handle pushes the pump piston down with a force of $84\ \text{N}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the pressure in the oil.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the upward force on the ram.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Each stroke pushes the pump piston down 6.0 cm. How far does the ram rise in one stroke?
parts.explanation: The area ratio is $\dfrac{4.5 \times 10^{-3}}{1.5 \times 10^{-4}} = 30$, so the ram rises $\dfrac{6.0}{30} = 0.2\ \text{cm}$.
parts.workedSolution: 1. The area ratio is $\dfrac{4.5 \times 10^{-3}}{1.5 \times 10^{-4}} = 30$, so the ram rises $\dfrac{6.0}{30} = 0.2\ \text{cm}$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: How many strokes are needed to raise the ram by 8.0 cm?

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why there is a one-way valve between the pump cylinder and the ram cylinder.

points.description: It stops oil flowing back from the ram cylinder when the handle is raised, so the load does not sink

explanation: p = F/A = 5.6 × 10⁵ Pa; F = pA = 2520 N; the ram rises 1/30 of the pump piston's movement per stroke (0.2 cm), so 40 strokes raise it 8.0 cm. The valve keeps the oil, and the load, up between strokes.
hints: Use p = F ÷ A, then F = p × A.
The volume of oil moved per stroke is the same in both cylinders.

stem: In a car braking system, what does the brake pedal push on directly?

options.content: The brake pads
options.rationale: The pads are pushed by the wheel cylinders.

options.content: The wheel cylinders
options.rationale: Brake fluid carries the pressure to the wheel cylinders.

options.content: A piston in the master cylinder
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The brake discs
options.rationale: The discs turn with the wheels.

explanation: The pedal pushes a piston into the master cylinder; the brake fluid passes the pressure to the wheel cylinders, which push the pads against the discs.

stem: A mechanic finds air bubbles in the brake fluid of a car. Why do they make the brakes weak and the pedal feel spongy?

options.content: Air makes the brake fluid freeze.
options.rationale: Air does not freeze brake fluid.

options.content: Air is denser than brake fluid and blocks the pipes.
options.rationale: Air is much less dense than the fluid.

options.content: Air is easily compressed, so pressing the pedal squashes the air instead of moving the wheel pistons.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Air bubbles increase the friction between the pads and discs.
options.rationale: The problem is in the fluid, not at the pads.

explanation: Liquids are almost incompressible, but air is not. Much of the pedal's movement goes into compressing the bubbles, so less pressure reaches the wheel cylinders. The brakes must be bled.
hints: Which is easier to squash: a liquid or a gas?

stem: In a car braking system the pistons in the wheel cylinders are wider than the piston in the master cylinder. What is the effect of this?

options.content: The pressure in the wheel cylinders is larger than in the master cylinder.
options.rationale: The pressure is the same everywhere in the fluid.

options.content: The wheel pistons move further than the master cylinder piston.
options.rationale: They move less far.

options.content: The brake fluid flows faster to the wheels.
options.rationale: This is not the effect of the wider pistons.

options.content: The force on each brake pad is larger than the force on the master cylinder piston.
options.rationale: Correct: the same pressure acts on a larger area.

explanation: The pressure is passed on equally, and force = pressure × area, so the wider wheel pistons push the pads with a larger force (moving a shorter distance).
hints: Pressure is passed on equally. Then use F = p × A.

stem: In a car braking system, the pressure in the brake fluid is the same at every wheel cylinder.
explanation: True. Pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is passed on equally, so all the wheel cylinders receive the same pressure and the wheels brake together.

stem: During the upstroke of a lift pump, what makes water from the well flow into the barrel below the piston?

options.content: Suction pulling the water up
options.rationale: Suction is not a force; the atmosphere pushes the water.

options.content: Atmospheric pressure acting on the water surface in the well
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The weight of the piston
options.rationale: The piston is rising; its weight does not push water up.

options.content: Water pressure from the spout
options.rationale: The spout is open to the air and is where water leaves.

explanation: As the piston rises, the pressure in the barrel below it falls. The greater atmospheric pressure on the water in the well pushes water up the pipe and through the inlet valve.

stem: During the downstroke of a lift pump, which valves are open and which are closed?

options.content: Inlet valve open; piston valve closed
options.rationale: This is the upstroke.

options.content: Inlet valve closed; piston valve open
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Both valves open
options.rationale: Water would then flow back into the well.

options.content: Both valves closed
options.rationale: The water in the barrel must pass through the piston.

explanation: On the downstroke the inlet valve closes so water cannot return to the well, and the piston valve opens so water passes through the piston to the space above it.
hints: Where must the water in the barrel go when the piston moves down?

stem: At a place where atmospheric pressure is $90\ \text{kPa}$, what is the greatest height to which atmospheric pressure can push water up the pipe of a lift pump? (Density of water $= 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$, $g = 10\ \text{N/kg}$.)
explanation: $h = \dfrac{p}{\rho g} = \dfrac{90\,000}{1000 \times 10} = 9.0\ \text{m}$.
hints: Use p = ρgh and rearrange for h.
Convert kPa to Pa: 1 kPa = 1000 Pa.

stem: When the handle of a bicycle pump is pushed in, when does the tyre valve open?

options.content: As soon as the handle starts to move
options.rationale: The barrel air must first be compressed above tyre pressure.

options.content: When the pressure of the air in the barrel becomes greater than the pressure in the tyre
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: When the air in the barrel reaches atmospheric pressure
options.rationale: Atmospheric pressure is lower than the tyre pressure.

options.content: Only when the handle is pulled out
options.rationale: On the pull stroke the tyre valve closes.

explanation: The air in the barrel is compressed until its pressure exceeds the tyre pressure; then the tyre valve opens and air is forced into the tyre.

stem: How does air get into the barrel of a bicycle pump when the handle is pulled out?

options.content: Air flows back out of the tyre through the tyre valve.
options.rationale: The tyre valve closes on the pull stroke.

options.content: Atmospheric pressure pushes outside air past the flexible edges of the washer, because the pressure in the barrel has fallen.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Air passes through tiny holes in the barrel wall.
options.rationale: The barrel is airtight.

options.content: The washer makes air.
options.rationale: Air comes from outside.

explanation: Pulling the handle increases the volume and lowers the pressure in the barrel. The tyre valve closes, and the higher atmospheric pressure pushes air past the flexible washer into the barrel.
hints: Compare the pressure inside the barrel with atmospheric pressure during the pull stroke.

stem: After pumping up a tyre, a cyclist notices that the barrel of the bicycle pump is warm. What is the main reason?

options.content: The tyre is hot and heats the pump.
options.rationale: The heat is produced in the pump itself.

options.content: Air expanding in the barrel heats it.
options.rationale: Expanding air cools; compressing it warms it.

options.content: The sun heats the metal barrel.
options.rationale: The warming happens even in the shade.

options.content: Work done compressing the air raises its temperature, and there is friction between the washer and the barrel.
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: Pushing the piston does work on the air, increasing its internal energy and temperature, and friction between the washer and the barrel wall also produces heat.
hints: Think about the energy transferred when you squash the air.

stem: Match each device with the correct description.

right.content: A lift pump that raises water from a well
A force pump that pushes air through an outlet valve
Carries liquid over a barrier to a lower level without a pump
Passes pressure through oil to lift a heavy load

explanation: Siphon: flow over a barrier; hydraulic jack: pressure in a liquid multiplies force; Blair pump: lift pump; bicycle pump: force pump.

stem: A family uses a lift pump with its barrel at ground level to draw water from a well.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe what happens during the upstroke of the pump.

points.description: The piston rises and its valve is closed by the water above it
The pressure in the barrel below the piston falls, so atmospheric pressure pushes water from the well up through the inlet valve into the barrel
The water above the piston is lifted and flows out of the spout

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: State the purpose of the inlet valve at the bottom of the barrel.

points.description: It stops water flowing back down into the well on the downstroke

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The water in another well is 15 m below the ground. Explain why this pump cannot raise water from that well.

points.description: Atmospheric pressure can only push water up about 10 m (less at altitude)
So the water cannot reach a barrel 15 m above it; the cylinder must be placed down in the water (or a different pump used)

explanation: Upstroke: the piston valve closes, the pressure below the piston falls, atmospheric pressure pushes water in, and water above the piston is lifted out. The inlet valve stops back-flow. Atmospheric pressure can only hold up about 10 m of water.
hints: Say what each valve is doing.
How high can atmospheric pressure push a column of water?

stem: On an irrigation scheme, farmers use plastic siphon tubes to carry water from a canal over its bank into field furrows that are lower than the water in the canal.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State two conditions needed for a siphon tube to work.

points.description: The tube must be completely full of water (no air) when it is started
The outlet must be lower than the water surface in the canal (and the bank less than about 10 m above the water)

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain, in terms of pressure, why water flows through the tube.

points.description: Atmospheric pressure on the canal surface pushes water up the short arm
The column of water on the outlet side is taller, so the pressure at the top of the tube is greater on the canal side and water is pushed towards the outlet

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest why the flow stops if the canal water level falls below the end of the tube.

points.description: Air enters the tube and breaks the column of water

explanation: A siphon needs a full tube and an outlet below the supply surface. Atmospheric pressure drives the water up; the taller outlet column means the pressure at the bend is greater on the supply side. Air entering breaks the column.
hints: Compare the heights of the two arms of the tube above their water levels.
